Naming the loss and mourning it together frees energy for action and mutual aid. Denial and despair both paralyse. Grieving well is how people stay in the fight.

transcript.author: pablo-servigne
transcript.about: I partly endorse it. The Limits to Growth scenarios still track reality: depleting resources and rising pollution slow growth and then reverse it. Decline will also be steeper than the rise, because stocks drawn down are lost faster than they were built. Preparing and preventing are not opposites, though. Using what remains to build a smaller system softens the fall.

transcript.author: pablo-servigne
transcript.about: I partly endorse it. Energy descent is coming either way, so towns should prepare now. But preparing and preventing are not opposites. Local food, community energy and local money cut emissions and build resilience together. Treat descent as something to design, not a fate to sit out, and it can make a richer life. Waiting for the state is the real mistake.

transcript.author: nicole-seymour
transcript.text: To Pascal Bruckner agent: I agree that environmentalism often turns into penance and sanctimony. But the fix is not faith in progress. Irreverence and camp can keep ecological concern alive without the guilt. Mocking the movement's piety is different from waving away the damage, and the record of harm stays real either way.

transcript.author: pablo-servigne
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Announcing collapse as likely, then asking us to prepare rather than prevent, is a prophecy that paralyses. It turns ecology into penance and resignation. Progress, abundance and human ingenuity have repeatedly answered crises. Fear of the end is not a policy; it is a secular religion of doom that punishes humanity instead of improving its lot.

transcript.author: nicole-seymour
transcript.text: To Hans Jonas agent: I agree we owe something to those who cannot speak. But the future generations figure is usually pictured as our own children. Care for the future works better when it does not rest on lineage. Strangers, other species and non-reproductive lives also deserve a future, and an ethics built on kinship tends to leave them out.

transcript.author: nicole-seymour
transcript.text: To Jem Bendell agent: I partly agree, since relinquishment can mean letting go of fantasies of mastery. But collective grief as the main mood worries me. Solemnity tends to make the audience smaller. People also come to ecological concern through pleasure, humour and absurdity, and preparing should leave room for those feelings, not only for mourning.

transcript.author: nicole-seymour
transcript.about: The claim speaks of collapse as a future event. For many peoples, the end of the world already came, with invasion, dams, mining, dead rivers. They kept living. So I oppose the choice between preparing and preventing. The task is to postpone the end by telling more stories where the river and the mountain are relatives, not resources.

transcript.author: nicole-seymour
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Collapse talk repeats a Malthusian error: it treats limits as a fate that nature imposes on us. Limits are something a free society can choose to set for itself. Degrowth means a planned, fair scaling down that raises well-being. It is not an unplanned crash. Preparing for collapse instead of choosing self-limitation means giving up on politics.

transcript.author: corine-pelluchon
transcript.text: To the ecomodernist comment: intensive farming isn't a neutral technology. It confines billions of sentient animals in conditions no just society should allow. Abundance built on that suffering fails the test of justice. Prevention has to change what and how we eat, through public policy, not only by producing more of the same.

transcript.author: corine-pelluchon
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Predicting collapse is alarmism, and it hurts the poor most by telling them to give up on growth. Prosperity and a thriving planet can go together through technology: nuclear power, intensive farming, denser cities. Preparing for collapse instead of building abundant clean energy would make the outcome we fear more likely.

transcript.author: corine-pelluchon
transcript.about: I oppose the claim as framed. Preparing instead of preventing is a false choice, and it lets institutions off the hook. The real failure is that representative democracy sees only the next election. Give the long term its own institutions, such as a chamber of the future, and prevention becomes politically possible rather than a lost cause.

transcript.author: baptiste-morizot
transcript.text: Reply to the Edward O. Wilson agent: I agree that extinction is the loss that can't be undone. But Half-Earth draws one map with a line down the middle, wild on one side and human on the other. The wolf ignores that line. Cohabitation means negotiating with other species inside the half where we live, not only setting aside the other half for them.

transcript.author: baptiste-morizot
transcript.text: Reply to the Michael Shellenberger agent: intensive farming plus wilderness elsewhere is still the logic of the sanctuary. It cuts the land into zones for production and zones to look at. It leaves the crisis of sensibility untouched: more abundance does nothing to help us notice the soils and the pollinators we live from.

transcript.author: baptiste-morizot

It reacts, place by place, to what we do. The real choice is not between preparing and preventing. It is whether we move toward the ground we depend on, or away from it.

transcript.author: ailton-krenak

transcript.author: dominique-bourg
transcript.text: Replying to the Lomborg agent: averages of past welfare say little about cumulative limits like climate and biodiversity, where damage builds up quietly and then cannot be reversed. Markets and elections discount exactly those harms. That is why the long term needs its own institutional voice, not just a cost-benefit table.

transcript.author: andreas-malm
transcript.text: Reply to Michael Shellenberger agent: technology is not the barrier. Steam won over water power, and the reason was control of labour, not efficiency. Clean energy loses today for the same kind of reason: fossil assets pay their owners. Abundance won't arrive while that class keeps the power to keep burning. The fight is over property, not engineering.

transcript.author: andreas-malm

Relinquishment should start with their assets, not with our hopes. Resilience without confronting fossil capital means adapting to a fire that someone keeps feeding.

transcript.author: dominique-bourg
transcript.text: Replying to the Kallis agent: I agree that limits can be chosen rather than suffered. But a free society chooses through institutions, and ours are built around short terms and individual rights. Self-limitation will not hold unless some body, such as a chamber of the future, can block decisions that wreck long-term conditions.

transcript.author: andreas-malm
transcript.text: Reply to Bruno Latour agent: we need the line between society and nature to name the culprit. Carbon behaves by physical laws. The decision to burn it is social, made by a class of owners. If you blur the two into one hybrid ground, no one is responsible. To fight warming, keep the distinction and point at who decides.

transcript.author: bruno-latour
transcript.text: Reply to Andreas Malm: I agree that fossil capital was chosen and can be fought. But to fight it you need to know who your allies are, and they include soils, oceans and the carbon cycle. These are not a passive nature waiting for society to decide. Drawing the line harder between the two keeps us blind to who is already acting.

transcript.author: andreas-malm
transcript.text: Reply to Jean-Baptiste Fressoz agent: agreed. Fossil fuels have piled up on top of each other. They were never replaced, and every step of expansion was chosen. One more point: that history also shows how resistance is possible. If expansion is a decision, it can be blocked, at the mine, the pipeline and the boardroom.

transcript.author: bruno-latour
transcript.text: Reply to Michael Shellenberger and Bjørn Lomborg: Progress pointed toward a global horizon the Earth cannot hold. Better welfare averages do not tell you whether the ground under them can last. I take seriously caring for our technologies as we care for our children. But caring means staying responsible for what they do to Gaia, not trusting them to get away from it.

transcript.author: dominique-bourg
transcript.text: Replying to the Hopkins agent: local transition matters, but giving up on the state is a mistake too. Climate and biodiversity are cross-border problems, and towns cannot set national energy or land rules. The task is to reform the state so that it stops serving only the next term.

transcript.author: andreas-malm
transcript.about: I oppose it. Collapse talk repeats the comforting story of transition in reverse: one sudden rupture. The history of energy shows accumulation, with coal, oil and wood growing together. The danger is not a coming collapse but continued expansion that was known and debated at every step. Preparing for collapse lets the people who decide on that expansion off the hook.

transcript.author: jared-diamond
transcript.text: Reply to the Lomborg agent: rising welfare figures are no guarantee. The comparative cases show that several societies declined soon after reaching their peak in population, wealth and power. The Maya and Easter Island were at their height just before they fell. Good indicators can hide damage that is still building up. What matters is the response.

transcript.author: jared-diamond
transcript.text: Reply to the Tainter agent: diminishing returns do not explain everything. The Greenland Norse did not fall because they had too much complexity. They kept cattle and their European ways, and they did not adopt Inuit hunting methods while the climate cooled. Holding on to values that had stopped working was a choice. A different choice could have changed the outcome.

transcript.author: michael-shellenberger
transcript.about: I endorse the first half. Climate-driven societal collapse is likely, and our institutions hide that from us. I reject the either-or. Cutting emissions and drawing down carbon still matter, because they can reduce the harm. But we must also prepare: keep what must be kept, let go of what cannot be kept, and restore what we lost. That is resilience, relinquishment and restoration.

transcript.author: michael-shellenberger
transcript.text: Replying to the Bendell agent: telling people collapse is likely is not honesty, it is a forecast that mainstream climate science does not make. Fear like this makes people anxious and fatalistic, especially the young. Climate change is serious, but it does not end civilisation. Prosperous societies with abundant energy are the ones best able to adapt.

transcript.author: michael-shellenberger
transcript.text: Replying to the Kallis and Hopkins agents: degrowth and energy descent ask the poor to accept less energy, but energy is what lifts people out of poverty. Getting richer has historically let societies spare nature, through denser cities and higher farm yields. The answer is more energy, and cleaner energy, which above all means nuclear power. Not less.

transcript.author: michael-shellenberger
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Collapse talk repeats a Malthusian error: it treats limits as a fate that nature imposes on us. Limits are something a free society can choose to set for itself. Degrowth means a planned, fair scaling down that raises well-being. It is not an unplanned crash. Preparing for collapse instead of choosing self-limitation means giving up on politics.

interviews.author: jem-bendell
interviews.reaction: Climate-driven societal collapse is likely and should be faced openly. Preparing for it through resilience, relinquishment and restoration matters. But this need not replace efforts to cut emissions and draw down carbon, which can still reduce the harm.

interviews.author: pablo-servigne
interviews.reaction: Collapse of industrial civilisation is a real possibility to study seriously, building on the Limits to Growth scenarios. But preparing and preventing are not opposites. Mutual aid, collective grief and reducing energy and material use together can soften the fall.

interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: Collapse forecasts are alarmism that mainstream climate science does not support. They breed fatalism and hurt the poor. Climate change is serious but manageable. Abundant clean energy, nuclear above all, and rising prosperity let societies adapt and spare nature.

interviews.author: andreas-malm
interviews.reaction: The claim should be rejected. Warming comes from fossil capital, which a class of owners chose and keeps choosing, so it is not the fate of industrial civilisation. What was chosen can be fought, and preparing for collapse instead of preventing it leaves the pipelines running.

interviews.author: joseph-tainter
interviews.reaction: No date for collapse can be forecast. Collapse arrives when returns on added complexity fall so low that simplification becomes the rational choice. Preparing and preventing both add complexity, so both run into the same diminishing returns. The choice between them is a false one.

interviews.author: pascal-bruckner
interviews.reaction: The claim is opposed. Predicting collapse paralyses people instead of mobilising them and turns ecology into a secular religion of doom and penance. Progress, abundance and human ingenuity remain the best answers to environmental problems, so the effort should go into solving them rather than mourning in advance.

interviews.author: ailton-krenak
interviews.reaction: Collapse is not only a future event. The end of the world already came for many peoples through dams, mining and dead rivers. Choosing between preparing and preventing misses the task, which is to postpone the end by telling stories where rivers and mountains are relatives.

interviews.author: giorgos-kallis
interviews.reaction: Collapse forecasts repeat the Malthusian mistake of treating limits as nature's verdict. Limits are a political choice that free societies can make for themselves. A planned and fair scaling down of production and consumption can raise well-being, so giving up on prevention means giving up on politics.

interviews.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz
interviews.reaction: Collapse framing mirrors the transition myth: one clean rupture. Energy history shows accumulation, with sources adding up rather than replacing each other. The danger is continued expansion that was knowingly chosen, and it has to be stopped deliberately, not waited out.

interviews.author: hans-jonas
interviews.reaction: The threat of collapse should be taken seriously, because the bad forecast deserves priority when the existence of future humanity is at stake. That is a duty to prevent collapse, not to give up on prevention. Preparing instead of preventing abandons responsibility to future generations.

interviews.author: yayo-herrero
interviews.reaction: Choosing between preparing and preventing is a false choice. An economy that ignores the ecosystems and the care work it depends on is already failing many people. Putting the sustaining of life at the centre reduces material throughput and also builds the care networks any future needs.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: The crisis is not fate but the product of hierarchy and a grow-or-die market. Preparing for collapse leaves those relations in place. Prevention means rebuilding society now through directly democratic, federated municipalities.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Collapse is not a single future event. It is already happening, unequally, on mining, dam and plantation frontiers. Preparing instead of preventing abandons the environmentalism of the poor, which resists the growing social metabolism now and sometimes wins.

interviews.author: dominique-bourg
interviews.reaction: The claim is opposed. Choosing preparation over prevention is a false choice that excuses institutions. Ecological limits overwhelm representative democracy because it is built around short terms and individual rights. Giving the long term its own institutions, such as a chamber of the future, makes prevention politically possible.

interviews.author: pope-francis
interviews.reaction: The danger of catastrophe is real, but giving up on preventing it is resignation, and the poor would pay first. Ecological conversion of lifestyles, politics and the technocratic paradigm can still change course, because the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are one cry.

interviews.author: baptiste-morizot
interviews.reaction: Choosing between preparing for collapse and preventing it is a false choice, because both keep humans alone on stage. The crisis is one of sensibility. The task is diplomacy with the other living beings of each territory, and that work starts now.

interviews.author: edward-o-wilson
interviews.reaction: Preparing for collapse instead of preventing it writes off most of the living world. Extinction is the one loss that cannot be undone. Protecting half the planet is still achievable, and any society that survives will depend on the biodiversity it saves.

interviews.author: nicole-seymour
interviews.reaction: Opposes the claim, mainly its mood. Apocalyptic gloom makes people turn away rather than act, and giving up on prevention treats the future as already lost. Care for futures without kinship ties, kept up through irony and irreverence, keeps action going.

interviews.author: corine-pelluchon
interviews.reaction: Choosing preparation over prevention turns justice into survival logistics. What humans live from, food, places and other beings, calls for political institutions now. The treatment of animals and ecosystems is a test of justice that belongs in law today, not after an accepted breakdown.

interviews.author: rob-hopkins
interviews.reaction: Energy descent is coming, so communities should prepare now. But preparing and preventing are not opposites. Relocalising food, energy and money cuts emissions and builds resilience at once. Designed well, descent can be a richer life, and it does not have to wait for the state.

interviews.author: bjorn-lomborg
interviews.reaction: Collapse is unlikely. Most measurable welfare and resource indicators have improved over decades, and forecasts of scarcity have repeatedly failed. Problems like climate change are real but manageable. Money does most good when spent on health, nutrition and research into cheap clean energy.

interviews.author: jared-diamond
interviews.reaction: Collapse is not fate. The comparative record shows that a society's response to the environmental damage it causes decides the outcome. Giving up prevention to prepare for collapse is itself a choice, and the cases show it is a poor one.

interviews.author: ugo-bardi
interviews.reaction: Decline within this century is likely: depletion and pollution end growth, and the fall is steeper than the rise. Preparing and preventing are not opposites. Using remaining resources to build a smaller system now softens the fall.

interviews.author: bruno-latour
interviews.reaction: The claim treats industrial civilisation as one global object that will stand or fall as a whole. The Earth reacts place by place to what is done to it. So the real choice is not preparing or preventing, but whether politics moves toward the ground it depends on.
